findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled on return
findings.body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection launch legacy writes in goroutines using context.WithTimeoutCause derived from the incoming request ctx. That parent context is owned by the API-server request and may be cancelled as soon as the handler returns the unified-storage result, racing with or cancelling the legacy write. The 10s timeout does not detach the goroutine from the parent. Consequently the supposedly protective legacy copy can silently never be written, especially for slower legacy stores. The legacy context should be detached (for example context.WithoutCancel/background-derived) while preserving values, with only the new timeout applied.

findings.title: Legacy goroutines race with the caller on the shared object
findings.body: Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the asynchronous Legacy.Create, while immediately returning `created` to the caller. The caller/serializer and the legacy store can therefore read or mutate the same underlying object concurrently (for example resource version, UID or timestamps set by a store). Update similarly shares `objInfo` with an asynchronous legacy call after the synchronous storage update has already consumed it. This is a data race and can produce corrupted or inconsistent legacy writes; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy/computed object.

findings.title: Mode 3 update no longer passes the storage-computed object to legacy
findings.body: Update now passes the original `objInfo` directly to Legacy.Update. A registry Update implementation recomputes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the old object it loads from legacy storage, so legacy recomputes the update against a different (possibly missing or stale) old object instead of applying the exact object already committed to unified storage, as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did. This can make the asynchronous legacy update fail (for example NotFound/conflict) or diverge from unified storage while the API call reports success. The computed/returned storage object should be wrapped and passed to legacy.

findings.title: Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) for elapsed storage time; Update does the same on storage failure (line 129). Delete records a successful storage duration using `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label (line 106), creating wrong/high-cardinality series. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration (line 166). Dashboards/alerts based on these metrics will attribute failures and latency to the wrong backend and cannot be used to verify mode 3 legacy health.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy failures are not logged
findings.body: The legacy goroutines in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection only feed a duration metric and discard the error otherwise. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy failures with object context. If the legacy safety copy fails in mode 3, operators have no log message identifying the kind/name/error to reconcile the divergence; only an aggregate metric counter changes. Each goroutine should log the returned error (without relying on the possibly-cancelled request logger).

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never wait for or verify the asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example Create at lines 30-32 and Update at lines 313-315) but return/assert immediately after the dual-writer call and never synchronize with the goroutine or call AssertCalled/AssertExpectations for the legacy mock. The tests therefore pass even if the legacy write is removed, cancelled, or never executes, and leaked goroutines can instead race with later tests using the shared mock/example objects. Tests need a synchronization/wait mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was invoked (and that failures are handled).

findings.title: Mode 3 integration test synchronously asserts legacy visibility after async writes
findings.body: The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes through the k8s API and immediately checks the legacy playlist API (for example the legacy list/get checks inside doPlaylistTests). Because mode 3 now performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines, there is no happens-before guarantee that the legacy row exists when those assertions run. This makes the new file/unified-storage mode 3 integration cases flaky and can also hide eventual-consistency behaviour that needs polling with a timeout instead of immediate equality assertions.
